summary: SWE-RPG is a repository-level issue-resolution benchmark of 163 tasks (85 Java, 78 Python; 31 repos; 113 bug fixes, 50 features) that adds validated reference artifacts for requirement clarification (implicit-requirement QA points in six categories derived from interviews with ten practitioners) and implementation plans (steps checked by having a coding agent reproduce each gold sub-patch). It evaluates Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode with six LLM backends, two runs each, and uses a GPT-5.6-Sol judge to attribute each failed run to its earliest deviating stage.

claims.claim: Popular coding agents average only 31.5% resolved; best configuration OpenCode + Kimi-K3 at 49.7%.
claims.evidence: §5.1 and Fig. 5; SWE-bench protocol (fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests); two runs per configuration, run-level aggregates; no CIs, no per-language breakdown.

claims.claim: Implicit-requirement recovery is the main bottleneck, accounting for 24.5-46.0% of runs.
claims.evidence: Fig. 6 stage attribution by GPT-5.6-Sol judge; judge matched human consensus on 46/50 sampled unresolved runs (92%). Attribution is against a single synthesized reference; because agents run autonomously and cannot ask questions, some 'requirement failures' may reflect underspecified issues rather than agent deficiency.

claims.claim: Agents identify where to edit but under-specify how to implement and verify; planning coverage cascades from target location to approach to constraints/validation.
claims.evidence: §5.3, Fig. 7: Claude Code 79.7% to 64.5% to 41.6%; Codex 65.6% to 49.0% to 37.1%; OpenCode 43.8% to 31.1% to 24.8%. Judge coverage decisions agree with humans in 96% of 50 sampled assessments.

claims.claim: Similar resolve rates can hide different failure profiles.
claims.evidence: §5.2: Codex vs Claude Code with DeepSeek-V4-Pro 40.5% vs 39.3% resolved; requirement failures 26.4% vs 40.5%; implementation failures 23.9% vs 7.4%.

patterns.note: Missing implicit requirements (interfaces, conventions, data-structure semantics) are the most common failure stage; argues for explicit acceptance criteria and constraints in task input.

Validated plans with constraints and validation strategy were sufficient for a coding agent to reproduce gold sub-patches during GT construction, and agents' own plans lack constraints/validation; indirect evidence that spec-first inputs would help, not tested as an intervention.
Plan quality is measured but planner-executor separation is not compared against single-loop agents.
SWE-bench-style benchmark extended with intermediate-stage references and Java tasks.
LLM judge used for stage attribution and coverage, validated on 50 samples each (92%, 96%); no inter-annotator agreement reported.

methodology.sample: 163 tasks from 31 repos (17 Java / 14 Python), filtered from 2,000+ issue-PR pairs; avg codebase 272.51K LOC; 3 agents x 6 LLMs x 2 runs.
methodology.baselines: Current agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) and current models (Claude-Sonnet-5, GPT-5.6-Terra, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GLM-5.2, MiniMax-M3, Kimi-K3); no human baseline.
methodology.models: Six LLM backends; GT synthesis by GPT-5.4; judge GPT-5.6-Sol.
methodology.variance: Two runs per configuration, aggregated; no variance or CIs reported.
methodology.ablations: None (no condition where agents receive clarification or plan GTs as input).
methodology.contamination_controls: Tasks required to be recent and non-overlapping with existing issue-resolution benchmarks; no explicit model-cutoff check.
methodology.languages: Java (85 tasks) and Python (78 tasks); no per-language results.

standards.artifacts: Benchmark data and evaluation code at github.com/Xin-Zhou-smu/SWE-RPG-Bench.

biases.detail: Judge validated only on 50-item samples with no inter-annotator agreement (admitted); GTs themselves synthesized by GPT-5.4 before human review.
Two runs per configuration, no spread reported; scaffold/model rankings differ by a few points.
'Requirement failure' is attributed to the agent, but agents could not ask for clarification; underspecified issues are conflated with agent weakness.
163 tasks split across two languages and two task types; per-language results not given.
OpenAI models build GTs and judge runs that include Codex/GPT backends; no evidence of favouritism (Codex is lowest agent), but not cross-checked with another judge.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and six commercial/open LLMs; no author vendor ties stated.
coi.funding: No acknowledgments or funding statement found.
coi.detail: Academic benchmark; authors do not ship a ranked system.

verdict_reason: Current agents and models, half-Java tasks, released artifacts, and a partially validated judge make this directly useful; caveats are two runs without variance, LLM-synthesized references, no intervention test, and attribution that cannot separate underspecified issues from agent failure.
applicability: High. Over half the tasks are Java and the agents studied are the same mixed hosts the team runs (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode). The main lesson backs spec-driven development: agents most often fail by missing implicit requirements, especially interface contracts, code conventions and data-structure semantics, and their plans omit constraints and validation steps. For cross-repository work across several repositories, specs should explicitly state cross-repo interface/DTO contracts, schema invariants, naming conventions and the tests that prove each change, rather than relying on the agent to infer them. The model and scaffold spread (17.8% to 49.7%) is also a reason to benchmark each host-model pair on the team's own Java tasks instead of assuming parity. The paper did not test giving agents the specs, so the size of the benefit is unknown.

conflicts_with.detail: SWE-Bench Pro Verified finds misleading problem statements and improperly scoped tests distort agent scores; SWE-RPG attributes the largest failure share to agents' implicit-requirement recovery without separating task underspecification, so part of that bottleneck may be benchmark-task quality.
